power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Yobe State MoH in implementing this study including their initiatives to ensure stakeholder engagement at the level of the State, Nguru and Karasuwa Local Government Areas, and at the community levels.
What are the new findings?
 SQ-LNS was an important source of motivation for caregivers to bring their children to health facilities, creating opportunities for vaccination.
 Persistent barriers to vaccination included socio-cultural misconceptions, gender norms, long waiting time and distance to health facilities.
 Sustained community engagement, including targeted male sensitization, is important to improve measles vaccination acceptability.

 Successful implementation of co-delivery programs also requires well-organized service delivery, with services decentralized to health facilities as close as possible to beneficiaries, particularly to reduce travel distances and waiting times.

text.text: These complementary benefits suggest that co-delivering preventive nutrition supplements with routine immunization could simultaneously address undernutrition and low vaccination coverage, yet evidence on such integrated strategies remains scarce.

The NutriVax-Measles trial showed that a strategy combining SQ-LNS supplementation and routine immunization services for children aged 6-23 months significantly increased measles vaccination uptake in Northern Nigeria (17).

text.text: The objective of this qualitative study was to assess the feasibility and acceptability of measles vaccination, SQ-LNS distribution, and the NutriVax strategy in Northern Nigeria and to identify factors that could inform future scale-up.
This study employed an exploratory qualitative research design nested in the NutriVax-Measles trial, following SRQR guidelines (Supplementary file 1).

Semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted from 16-May to 30-July 2025 among various stakeholders in both health system (healthcare workers, community health workers) and community (parents/caregivers and community representatives).
The NutriVax-Measles study was a pediatric pragmatic superiority parallel cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in Yobe State, Northeastern Nigeria.

The main objective was to evaluate an innovative intervention designed to improve measles vaccination coverage among children aged 6-23 months by distributing SQ-LNS alongside routine vaccinations at primary health care centers (Figure 1).

text.text: The intervention was implemented from July 2024 to July 2025 in Karasuwa and Nguru Local Government Areas (LGAs): each LGA comprised ten wards (clusters), five assigned for the intervention arm (NutriVax arm) and five for the control arm.
A comprehensive study protocol detailing all study objectives, eligibility criteria, and methodological approach has been published previously (19).
text.formatted: A comprehensive study protocol detailing all study objectives, eligibility criteria, and methodological approach has been published previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: All clusters followed the National Programme on Immunization (NPI) schedule, providing routine vaccination activities at Primary Health Care Centres (PHCCs) or Health Posts (HPs), with vaccines administered by Ministry of Health (MoH) staff according to MoH plans.

Community engagement and mobilization were provided by Community Nutrition Mobilizers (CNMs) at health facilities and within communities, to sensitize caregivers and promote vaccination, infant and young child feeding and dietary diversity following standardized procedures.

In the NutriVax clusters, caregivers of children aged 6-23 months received additional messages on SQ-LNS eligibility, and that they could receive monthly rations of one sachet of SQ-LNS per day for up to one year or until reaching 24 months of age, at the PHCC on specific session days.

Several adaptations to intervention implementation were introduced during the trial, including: improving the SQ-LNS-vaccination circuit to reduce waiting times; improve the comfort of waiting areas with the construction of shaded areas; forming men's groups and engaging community and religious leaders to increase awareness of the benefits of vaccination in both trial arms and of SQ-LNS in the intervention arm; working with MoH authorities to improve the availability of paracetamol for managing post-vaccination side effects; and providing up to three-months of SQ-LNS rations to reduce the frequency of visits for caregivers living far from PHCCs.

This qualitative study was conducted in 12 of the 20 wards included in the NutriVax-Measles trial, with six wards purposively selected from each LGA (three in the NutriVax arm and three in the control arm).
Wards were selected to capture variation in health centers access (Supplementary file 2).

Four stakeholder groups participated in the study: (1) parents or guardians of children aged 6-23 months, (2) health care workers (HCWs), (3) community health workers (CHWs), and (4) community representatives.

The qualitative study included IDIs with participants from each stakeholder group across all selected wards in both trial arms, as well as two FGDs per stakeholder group, with one conducted in each LGA, including participants from intervention wards only.

text.text: In addition, a gender lens was considered during development of the guides, to explore how gender norms, household roles, and decision-making dynamics influenced care-seeking behavior, vaccination uptake, and participation in SQ-LNS distribution.
The interview guides were first drafted in English, translated into Hausa by a professional translator, and pre-tested to ensure contextual and linguistic clarity.
Thematic saturation was assessed during weekly analytical debriefings, during which emerging themes were reviewed across completed interviews and discussions.
Data collection continued until these weekly reviews indicated that no new themes or insights were emerging from additional interviews or discussions.

All qualitative data were collected by a team of four trained qualitative research assistants (SAK, AMS, AGG, AG), all from Northern Nigeria, under the supervision of the social science research manager, also Nigerian (AS) and a French senior researcher (MP).

Engagement was also supported by a national steering committee bringing together MoH representatives at federal, state and local levels, nutrition and immunization partners, and community leaders.

The following results present key facilitators and barriers influencing the acceptability and feasibility 292 of measles vaccination and SQ-LNS distribution as part of the NutriVax-Measles trial across multiple 293 levels.

Findings are organized according to four main domains: (i) individual perceptions of vaccination, 294 SQ-LNS, and the NutriVax strategy; (ii) social influence and community engagement, highlighting the 295 role of community leaders, awareness campaigns, and male decision-makers; (iii) the quality and 296 organization of health services supporting intervention delivery; and (iv) remaining structural and 297 logistical barriers.
This structure allows for a comprehensive understanding of how the intervention 298 was perceived, implemented, and experienced in the field.
Most caregivers from both arms perceived vaccination as an effective means for preventing common vaccine-preventable diseases like measles and other childhood illnesses.

Some also described that past experiences with outbreaks of measles and diphtheria, as well as fear of disease complications (e.g., blindness in measles) positively influenced their perceptions of immunization and served as a motivator for them to vaccinate their children.
However, in both arms, a few participants strongly held misconceptions that vaccines cause infertility.
Others expressed concerns about post-immunization effects like fever, swelling, or children becoming irritable.
To address this latest fear, collaboration with LGA and facility officials was strengthened to ensure a steady supply of paracetamol after vaccination in both arms.

SQ-LNS was also widely accepted by parents and caregivers in the NutriVax arm, who appreciated its perceived benefits for appetite, child health, and overall well-being of children after consistent use.
Nearly all caregivers interviewed found the taste of SQ-LNS acceptable, and no HCWs reported any challenge related to it.
Caregivers also found it easy to give to their children, either taken directly from the sachet or mixed with food.
"Since I started giving it, my child became more active and eats more food.
I don't stop because I want him to continue being healthy."-(FGD, Parents, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm) A few mothers admitted to sharing the supplement with ineligible siblings within their family.
Others declared to share their child ration outside their family under a system whereby each mother takes turns to distribute to other mothers who are not beneficiaries of the programme.
Some SQ-LNS distributors also noted a few parents were borrowing children to obtain extra sachets.
Yet, participants indicated that the small sachet design discouraged sales.
"The others [children] at home also want it, so I just give them small from the child's own." -(IDI, Parents, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm) "Because of its small size, some people don't sell it.
Leaving it small is better.
If it becomes large, that is when they will sell it.
The small one is cheaper; it's the bigger one they usually sell.
Right now, the big one [Ready-to-use therapeutic food: RUTF] is sold for ₦450 per sachet, but this small one [SQ-LNS] is sold for ₦60 in the market." -(IDI, Parent, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm)
Many caregivers from the NutriVax arm appreciated receiving SQ-LNS during the same day of vaccination sessions and explained that it gave them a tangible reason to maintain vaccination schedules.

All interviewees from both community and health system indeed shared that the NutriVax strategy enhanced care-seeking behavior and acceptability of health facility visits, encouraging many parents who were previously hesitant to bring their children for immunization.
"When they gave the supplement, I saw that my child was eating well and became strong.

That made me happy to continue coming for vaccination because I knew both helped my child." -(IDI, Parents, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm) "Yes, it's now easier to take children to the facility because this support [SQ-LNS] being given motivates them to go.
In the past, you will find a child and their mother lying at home … the child is sick, no money for transport, no money for treatment …and they would say they would not go to the hospital.
But now that this is being provided, it has greatly improved their children's health." -(IDI, Community Health Workers, Nguru LGA, NutriVax Arm).

As planned in the standard operational procedures, CNMs and volunteers organized several routine health education during immunization days in both arms as well as on session days when SQ-LNS was distributed in NutriVax arms.

All interviewees agreed that such community mobilization was a key to reinforce awareness on vaccination and infant and young child feeding good practices in both arms, and on SQ-LNS in NutriVax arm, and encouraged caregivers to access healthcare facilities.
, there are people from their team who go house to house, sensitizing community members and encouraging them to go to the hospital and explaining the benefits of doing so.
Seeing this has truly increased the number of people going to the hospital now compared to the past." -(IDI, Community representative, Nguru LGA,
Community leaders also brought their children first for vaccination, which helped build trust and enhance the acceptability of measles vaccination within the community in both arms.
Some caregivers further explained that sharing success stories or attending healthcare facilities in groups motivated others to participate in the NutriVax programme.
The traditional leader even starts by gathering his own children and grandchildren to get them vaccinated first.
If there were any problem, it would happen to his children first.
That is why it has been done not just once or twice, and no such problems have been seen.
So even if someone tries to spread rumors, people don't believe them." -(IDI, Community representative, Karasuwa LGA, Control Arm)
In addition to the social influence and community engagement, gender norms were central in shaping care-seeking behavior in both trial arms.
In the majority of families, fathers were the ones who made decisions regarding family care and provided money to cover transportation expenses.
While most mothers required spousal approval before taking a child to the health center for vaccination, some men had negative perceptions regarding vaccines at the beginning of the trial.

In response to that barrier, CNMs, religious leaders, and community representatives targeted and sensitized men at places where they gathered to socialize, markets where they conducted business, and mosques where they prayed in congregation.
Several caregivers explained that fathers were thus more supportive, while some even accompanied their wives to facilities.
"Honestly, in the past, men were against taking children for vaccinations.
If a woman tried, it could even cause serious issues in the marriage.

But now, after repeated sensitization, they [men] understand the benefits of vaccines and will even be the ones to remind their wives that it's time to take the child." -(FGD, Parent, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm) Yet, some households still practiced traditional decision-making patterns at the end of the trial, as reported by a HCW.
The resulting increase in attendance initially created challenges related to workload, waiting times, and service organization.
Operational adjustments implemented over the course of the trial to reduce waiting time and improve the comfort of waiting areas were appreciated by stakeholders in both arms.

Ultimately, participants' accounts from the intervention arm indicated that co-delivery of vaccination and SQ-LNS was operationally feasible after adaptations were made to the organization of health services.

"It [workload] has really increased, because in the past, we used to wait for the women to come but now every Monday, they come in their numbers for measles vaccination… before now, we closed at the latest by two o'clock, but now we reach up to three or even five in the evening In both arms, some caregivers, especially those in distant settlements still faced challenges related to poor road conditions, seasonal flooding, or heat.
During the rainy season, roads to facilities often became impassable, forcing caregivers to postpone visits.
Additionally, caregivers coming from distant settlements struggled with transportation costs, and they found it difficult to reach health facilities, particularly in emergency situations.

Nevertheless, several interviewees reported that some parents, even if not all, manage to go to the healthcare centres for their children's health, especially in the intervention arm where SQ-LNS was provided for free.
"In rural areas, distance and poverty are major issues.
Some parents may want to bring their sick child but have nothing to eat themselves, let alone money for transport.

They just sit and watch the child because they cannot afford to take them to the hospital." -(FGD, Community representative, Nguru LGA, NutriVax arm) "You know, with the current economic situation in Nigeria, many people don't have money.

The provision of two-to three-month SQ-LNS rations for caregivers from remote areas, introduced during implementation to reduce the frequency of healthcare facility visits, was appreciated by parents.
"For those who come from distant villages, we give them two-or three-months' ration at once so that they do not have to come every month.
That has really helped because transport is costly for them." -(IDI, Community Health Worker, Karasuwa LGA, NutriVax arm)

Overall, our findings showed that combining SQ-LNS distribution with routine measles immunization services was acceptable to caregivers, communities, and health-system stakeholders, and feasible to implement within primary healthcare services.
However, successful implementation of both measles vaccination and SQ-LNS required adaptations to address barriers operating at individual, social, healthsystem, and structural levels (Figure 3).

text.text: Gender norms remained a key determinant of care-seeking.
Many mothers reported requiring spousal approval before bringing their children to be vaccinated.
Similar findings have been documented across African settings (40), including evidence from Ghana showing higher vaccination coverage when men were engaged in health-related decisions (41).

text.text: In the NutriVax trial, initial concerns among fathers were addressed through targeted sensitization activities conducted in social and religious gathering spaces, following which participants reported increased male support for immunization.

These findings emphasize that improving childhood vaccination coverage requires engaging not only mothers but also other household decision-makers for the long-term success of child health interventions in northern Nigeria and similar settings.

From a health-system perspective, the findings suggest that combining SQ-LNS distribution with routine immunization was feasible, but that feasibility was supported in part by iterative adaptations made during implementation rather than being an inherent feature of the original intervention package.
Increased caregiver attendance initially resulted in longer waiting times in PHCCs were SQ-LNS was provided, and higher workloads for healthcare workers.
In response, adaptations were introduced to improve registration systems, patient flow and waiting areas, and these changes were positively perceived by both healthcare workers and caregivers.
These findings highlight the importance of adaptive implementation when increased demand may place additional pressure on existing health-system capacity.

While SQ-LNS was distributed only in PHCCs within the NutriVax-Measles trial, the decentralization within smaller health facilities would likely have helped balance the additional workload, and to some extent, alleviate overcrowding at PHCCs.

Co-delivery of nutrition and immunization services should therefore not be viewed simply as the addition of a new service, but as an intervention that may require ongoing adjustment and strategic investment in service organization to respond to emerging implementation challenges.
This interpretation is consistent with previous literature suggesting that service-level and organizational interventions can improve patient experience and healthcare delivery outcomes (42).

text.text: In this context, HCWs and SQ-LNS distributors were specifically trained to improve interpersonal skills and make sure they have a respectful attitude.
Caregivers subsequently expressed high satisfaction . with the quality of interactions at health facilities.
Such capacity-building approaches may require repeated reinforcement to support sustained changes in provider behavior over time.

Persistent structural, geographical, and logistical barriers, including long distances between home and health facilities as well as competing household priorities, also limited equitable access to vaccination and SQ-LNS, as also found in the quantitative findings (17).

text.text: Distance to health facilities, poor road conditions, seasonal flooding, and transportation costs remained important challenges, especially since many caregivers lived in remote settlements and had limited economic resources.
These findings are consistent with previous studies identifying geographical and financial constraints as major barriers to vaccination uptake in African settings (40, (44) (45) (46).

text.text: In addition, competing livelihood and household priorities, including farming activities and market days, limited caregivers' availability to attend health facilities, particularly during peak farming periods.

These opportunity costs represent important determinants of healthcare utilization (12, 47, 48), and demonstrate that positive perceptions of an intervention alone are insufficient to overcome broader structural constraints.

text.text: Several adaptations were implemented in PHCCs where SQ-LNS was distributed, to mitigate these barriers, including providing two-to three-month SQ-LNS rations (instead of a one-month ration) for caregivers living far from health facilities, as was anticipated in the study protocol, as well as prioritizing them in the queue during visits.
Although these adaptations could not fully eliminate access constraints, they reduced the frequency of required visits and improved the feasibility of participation for vulnerable households.
Future scale-up strategies should consider such context-specific adaptations to ensure equitable access.
The results also highlight the importance of decentralizing the distribution of SQ-LNS to smaller health facilities, where immunization activities are routinely conducted, to improve accessibility.
This study adds evidence on the acceptability and feasibility of combining measles vaccination with SQ-LNS distribution in West Africa.

The inclusion of stakeholders from both community and healthsystem levels provided a comprehensive understanding of the NutriVax intervention implementation, and the convergence of findings across these stakeholder groups strengthens the validity of the results.

Data collection by local qualitative research assistants fluent in local languages likely facilitated trust, reduced interpretation bias and enabled a more contextually grounded understanding of participants' perceptions and experiences.
The use of established conceptual frameworks further supported a systematic interpretation of barriers and facilitators to measles vaccination and SQ-LNS implementation.
Yet, this study has several limitations.
First, the qualitative analysis was mainly based on a rapid thematic approach using interview summaries rather than systematic coding of full transcripts.

This approach was selected to allow timely feedback during implementation but may have reduced . analytical granularity and limited the identification of more nuanced perspectives in participants' narratives; nevertheless, the transcripts made it possible to retrieve the most relevant quotes following the rapid analysis to illustrate the different findings.
Second, FGDs were conducted only among participants from intervention wards, limiting direct comparison of group-level perspectives between intervention and control arms.

In addition, social desirability bias cannot be excluded, although the consistency of findings across different stakeholder groups provides some reassurance regarding the robustness of the major themes.

This study showed that co-delivering preventive SQ-LNS with routine immunizations was acceptable and feasible at primary healthcare settings in an insecure, resource-constrained context in Northern Nigeria that faces persistent high malnutrition rates and low vaccination coverage.
The perceived benefits for children's health, along with the convenience of receiving both services in a single visit, contributed to the intervention's acceptability within the community.
The findings also highlight the importance of adapting intervention delivery to address implementation barriers.

Future scale-up of such integrated care models in settings facing a similar dual threat to child survival will require sustained investment in community mobilization, including targeted sensitization efforts focused on men; health-system capacity-building; and structural efforts to decentralize the provision of SQ-LNS alongside immunization services, bringing them as close as possible beneficiaries to improve equitable access to care.

This approach comprised several steps to enable timely synthesis of insights: (1) each interview was conducted by a team of two research assistants: one serving as the interviewer and the other one as the note-taker.

A thematic summary grid template(27), specific to each stakeholder group was used to summarize key enablers, barriers, and adaptations across themes and subthemes simultaneously during participant interview (Supplementary file 4); (2) following each day of fieldwork, debriefing meetings were conducted between the social science research manager (SIA) and the qualitative research assistants, during which the team completed a global summary matrix organized by stakeholder group; (3) weekly debriefing meetings were conducted between the social science research manager (SIA), the NutriVax research manager (JN), and a senior researcher (MP) to review completed matrices, discuss patterns . across stakeholder groups, and refine interpretations; (4) the conceptual frameworks (Supplementary file 5) guided the systematic and contextually grounded interpretation of findings, which were subsequently organized at the individual, social, health-system and structural levels; (5) audio recordings were transcribed and simultaneously translated from Hausa to English, allowing the transcripts to complement the rapid qualitative analysis with relevant illustrative quotations.
